sentences.text: The only known species, Volgatitan simbirskiensis, is known from seven tail vertebrae belonging to a single individual.
Every vertebra possesses a strong crest on the ventral surface of the body, which is the only known unique trait of this taxon.
The estimated average mass of Volgatitan is 17.3 metric tons.
Volgatitan is the oldest known titanosaur from the Northern Hemisphere.
In 1982, Soviet scientist Vladimir Efimov discovered large bones embedded in pyrite nodules near the village of Slate Rudnik while searching for fossils along the right bank of the Volga River.
A total of seven fragmentary vertebrae were extracted from the fossil site.
Volgatitan was first described in November 2018 by Russian paleontologists Alexander Averianov and Vladimir Efimov.

The genus name Volga honors the river where the fossils were found, while the suffix 'titan' refers to divine beings from Greek mythology, and the specific name simbirskiensis honors Simbirsk, the former name of the city Ulyanovsk.
While initially classified as a titanosaur related to Lognkosauria, later studies suggest Volgatitan may belong to the family Mamenchisauridae.
A 2026 phylogenetic analysis by Mannion and Carvalho placed Volgatitan within the family Mamenchisauridae.
A phylogenetic analysis by Averianov and Efimov identified Volgatitan as a member of the clade Lithostrotia.
Volgatitan is the first European representative and the geologically oldest member of the Lithostrotian lineage, which previously contained only South American species.
The discovery suggests the Lithostrotian lineage leading to Lognkosauria had a much wider distribution than previously thought and went extinct everywhere except South America by the Late Cretaceous.
The Paleobiology Database lists Volgatitan's parent group as Mamenchisauridae.
Volgatitan lived during the Early Cretaceous in the Ulyanovsk Oblast of Russia.
Volgatitan lived between 136 and 130 million years ago, spanning the Hauterivian to Barremian stages of the Early Cretaceous.
